---
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/healthchecks/healthchecks
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: healthchecks/healthchecks:v4.3
  port: 8000
  vm: m1.medium
  flavor_id: "3"
  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2")
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0452
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: healthchecks
quirks:
  - "PULL THE PINNED IMAGE, DO NOT BUILD. healthchecks/healthchecks:v4.3 on Docker Hub, published 2026-07-14, and note the leading v on the tag. ⚠️ THE UPSTREAM COMPOSE BUILDS FROM SOURCE: its web service has a build section and the pre-built image line is commented out. Copy that file as-is onto redu and you get a from-source Python build with wheels for uwsgi, psycopg and mysqlclient on the app VM, for no benefit. Use the one-service compose in this file."
  - "⛔⛔ DEBUG DEFAULTS TO TRUE IN THE CODE, NOT FALSE. hc/settings.py:69 is envbool(\"DEBUG\", \"True\"). Upstream's .env.example sets it to False, so anyone who writes their own environment instead of copying that file ships a public Django with full tracebacks, settings and SQL on every error page. SET DEBUG=False EXPLICITLY. It also matters for the next quirk: Django only enforces ALLOWED_HOSTS when DEBUG is False."
  - "⛔⛔ SECRET_KEY DEFAULTS TO THE THREE-CHARACTER STRING --- , WHICH IS PUBLIC. hc/settings.py:66. Django signs session cookies, password-reset tokens and the instant-login links Healthchecks emails with that key, so leaving the default on a public hostname means anyone can mint a login link for any account. Generate a long random value, set it, and REUSE THE SAME VALUE ON EVERY REDEPLOY: changing it signs out every user and invalidates every login link already in someone's inbox. There is also a SECRET_KEY_FILE variant (settings.py:46-63) if you would rather mount it than pass it as an environment variable."
  - "⛔⛔ THE SQLITE FALLBACK IS SILENT AND HAS A SECOND TRAP INSIDE IT. hc/settings.py:206-215 defaults to SQLite at /opt/healthchecks/hc.sqlite, and Postgres is used ONLY when DB=postgres (:219). The trap: in the SQLite branch DB_NAME is the SQLITE FILE PATH. So a deploy that sets DB_HOST, DB_NAME, DB_USER and DB_PASSWORD but forgets DB=postgres comes up perfectly healthy, ignores the managed database entirely, and writes to a SQLite file NAMED AFTER YOUR DATABASE inside the container. Everything is lost on the next redeploy. Healthchecks also does NOT read DATABASE_URL, so redu's injected URL is useless here: map the five DB_* variables yourself. PROVE IT AFTER BOOT, BOTH HALVES: run `./manage.py shell -c \"from django.db import connection; print(connection.vendor, connection.settings_dict['NAME'], connection.settings_dict['HOST'])\"` in the container and confirm it prints postgresql plus the private DB host (the positive half, which is also what proves your exec reached the right container), THEN confirm /opt/healthchecks/hc.sqlite does NOT exist. The absence alone means nothing if the first command errored."
  - "⛔⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR: nobody, until you run one command, and the default lets strangers in beside you. There is no install wizard, no default account and no first-visitor-wins signup for admin. You create the account with `./manage.py createsuperuser` INSIDE the container, at deploy time. But REGISTRATION_OPEN defaults to True (settings.py:73), which means that until you set it False any stranger who finds the hostname can create their own ordinary account on your instance, with their own projects and their own outbound notifications. SET REGISTRATION_OPEN=False BEFORE THE FIRST BOOT, then create the superuser. ⚠️ SIGN IN WITH THE EMAIL ADDRESS, NOT THE USERNAME: hc/accounts/backends.py:43-61 looks the user up by email and ignores the Django username entirely, so a superuser created without an email address can never log in."
  - "TEST THAT REGISTRATION IS CLOSED, AND MIND THE POLARITY: 403 IS THE GOOD ANSWER. With REGISTRATION_OPEN=False, hc/accounts/views.py:210-220 makes an anonymous GET of /accounts/signup/csrf/ return HTTP 403, and it returns 200 with a token when signup is open. It is a GET with no side effects, so it is safe to probe. A script that treats 200 as success there has the polarity backwards and can never fail."
  - "⛔ WHICH URLS ARE MEANT TO BE WORLD-REACHABLE, AND WHICH ARE NOT. THIS APP EXISTS TO RECEIVE ANONYMOUS REQUESTS, so do not try to lock the whole hostname down. PUBLIC BY DESIGN: /ping/<uuid> and its /start, /fail, /log and /<exitstatus> suffixes, plus /ping/<ping-key>/<slug>; the signed status badges under /badge/...; and GET /api/v3/status/, which returns the two bytes OK. NOT PUBLIC: everything under /accounts/ except the login page, the whole of /admin/ (and hc/urls.py:16 replaces the Django admin login form with the ordinary one), the REST API under /api/v1|v2|v3/checks/ and friends, which needs an X-Api-Key header, /api/v3/metrics/, which is 403 unless METRICS_KEY is set and the X-Metrics-Key header matches, and the per-project Prometheus endpoint, which needs a 32-character read-only project key. The ping URLs are unguessable UUIDs and that is the whole security model: anyone holding one can mark a check up or down, so treat them as secrets."
  - "⛔ SITE_ROOT IS NOT COSMETIC, IT GENERATES EVERY PING URL. hc/settings.py:269 sets PING_ENDPOINT to SITE_ROOT + /ping/ , and :279-285 derives ALLOWED_HOSTS from SITE_ROOT's host when ALLOWED_HOSTS is unset. Get it wrong and every ping URL the UI hands out points at http://localhost:8000, which the user pastes into a crontab where it silently never reports. The value must be known before the container starts, so GENERATE THE DNAME YOURSELF up front in full healthchecks-<8 lowercase alphanumeric>.redu.cloud form and set SITE_ROOT to https:// plus that exact name. Set ALLOWED_HOSTS to the same hostname as well rather than relying on the derivation; a host Django does not recognise is answered with 400 Bad Request, which reads like a broken deploy."
  - "⚠️ IF THE LOGIN FORM ANSWERS 403 CSRF, IT IS THE PROXY HEADER, AND UPSTREAM SAYS SO. docker/README.md:98-115: this image's uWSGI decides whether a request is secure from the X-Forwarded-Proto header, and without it Django sees an http request carrying an https Origin and rejects every POST with \"CSRF verification failed\". redu terminates TLS in front of the container, so if you see that, set SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER=HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO,https, which hc/settings.py:77-78 parses as a comma-separated pair. The login script in this file exercises exactly that request, so you find out during the deploy rather than from the user."
  - "NO VOLUME IS NEEDED, AND THIS IS DELIBERATE. Static files are collected and compressed at image build time (Dockerfile:43-44), migrations run at every start, and hc/api/models.py:561-584 stores ping bodies in the DATABASE unless S3_BUCKET is set. Nothing durable is written to the container filesystem. The /data directory the Dockerfile creates is an empty convenience for SQLite users and is unused here. ⚠️ The flip side: PING_BODY_LIMIT defaults to 10000 bytes and every one of those bytes lands in your managed Postgres, so a fleet of chatty jobs grows the database rather than a disk you can see."
  - "NO migrate_command IS NEEDED. docker/uwsgi.ini:33 runs manage.py migrate as a uWSGI pre-app hook on every start, and the same file attaches sendalerts and sendreports as daemons inside the one container. So a single service really does run the web app, the alerting loop and the reports loop. If the container cannot reach the database at boot, the migrate hook fails and uWSGI exits, which restart:unless-stopped will retry: check the container log rather than assuming a crash loop is a bug in the recipe."
  - "⛔ DO NOT SET SMTPD_PORT ON redu. docker/uwsgi.ini:38-39 starts an inbound SMTP listener when it is set, which is how the \"ping a check by sending it an email\" feature works. redu proxies exactly ONE HTTP port per surface and does not route inbound mail to a VM, so that feature cannot work here and enabling it just opens a listener nobody can reach. Leave PING_EMAIL_DOMAIN alone too. OUTBOUND email is a different thing and does work: set EMAIL_HOST, EMAIL_PORT, EMAIL_HOST_USER, EMAIL_HOST_PASSWORD, EMAIL_USE_TLS and DEFAULT_FROM_EMAIL against any relay."
  - "OUTBOUND EMAIL IS OPTIONAL FOR LOGIN AND ESSENTIAL FOR ALERTS. Password login always works, so unlike some apps this one is usable with no relay at all; the emailed magic-link form is simply hidden when EMAIL_HOST is unset (hc/accounts/views.py:199). But a monitoring tool that cannot send anywhere is decoration, and the default email notification channel needs a working relay to even verify its address (EMAIL_USE_VERIFICATION defaults True). Ask the user which channel they actually want, and remember Healthchecks also speaks Slack, Telegram, ntfy, Gotify, Matrix, webhooks and about thirty others, most of which need only an outbound HTTPS call."
  - "⛔ LEAVE SHELL_ENABLED AND INTEGRATIONS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_IPS AT FALSE. Both default to False (hc/settings.py:397 and :431) and both should stay there. SHELL_ENABLED lets any logged-in user attach a notification that runs an arbitrary shell command inside the container. INTEGRATIONS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_IPS lets a webhook notification target a private address, which on redu means the user's own managed database VM. Turning either on is a decision the user makes explicitly, never a default you inherit."
  - "SIZING IS AN ESTIMATE AND UPSTREAM PUBLISHES NO NUMBER. The container runs four uWSGI worker processes plus the sendalerts and sendreports daemons, all Python with apprise, minio and psycopg loaded. m1.medium (2 vCPU / 4 GB) is the reasoned floor, and it is deliberately not the cheapest option because this app failing quietly means the user's monitoring stops without telling them. The documented way down is UWSGI_PROCESSES=2 (docker/README.md), which would make m1.small viable at GBP 0.0348/hr, about GBP 25.40 a month, instead of GBP 0.0452/hr. Offer that as the user's choice; measure the real figure on the first run and write it back."
  - "DELETE THE BUNDLED DATABASE FROM THE UPSTREAM COMPOSE. Its db service is a postgres:16 whose password comes from the same .env as the app's, on the same VM as the app. redu's managed Postgres replaces it with a separate private VM that survives the deployment."
  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> show the user the plan and the cost (about GBP 0.045/hr, roughly GBP 33 a month; inside the no-card free trial) and WAIT for their yes -> deploy_compose with flavor_id '3' (m1.medium), database:'managed', db_engine:'postgres', db_flavor_id:'2' (m1.small), port 8000, and dname set to the name you generated. Pass SECRET_KEY, SITE_ROOT, ALLOWED_HOSTS and the email settings through deploy_compose's env argument, which appends them to the project .env for interpolation. ⚠️ Pass flavor_id explicitly: plan_deploy upsizes a compose stack once needs_compose is declared, and nothing here is built from source. Pass db_flavor_id explicitly too, or the database VM defaults to the app flavor and doubles the bill."
  - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE, NOT GIT. Nothing is built. Write the compose file locally, then prepare_upload -> run the returned tar+curl block -> deploy_compose with the source_token and no repo. Cloning the upstream repo would hand deploy_compose a compose file that builds from source, which is the opposite of what you want."

Cron jobs and scheduled tasks that tell you when they ran, and shout when they did not. One Django
container, a managed Postgres, a public HTTPS URL. About GBP 33 a month.

## What this deploys

- **Healthchecks** from the official image, pinned to `v4.3`, on one m1.medium VM, port 8000. One
  container runs the web app, the alerting daemon and the reports daemon.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM: checks, ping history, accounts.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.
- **No volume.** Nothing durable is written to the container filesystem.

About GBP 0.045/hour. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Healthchecks on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## What is meant to be public here, and what is not

This app exists to receive anonymous HTTP requests, so "lock the hostname down" is the wrong
instinct. The split:

| Reachable by anyone, by design | Closed |
|---|---|
| `/ping/<uuid>` and `/ping/<uuid>/start`, `/fail`, `/log`, `/<exitstatus>` | `/admin/` and everything under `/accounts/` bar the login page |
| `/ping/<ping-key>/<slug>` and its suffixes | `/[REDACTED:value]` and the rest of the REST API (needs `X-Api-Key`) |
| the signed status badges under `/badge/...` | `/api/v3/metrics/` (403 unless `METRICS_KEY` matches) |
| `GET /api/v3/status/`, which returns the two bytes `OK` | `/accounts/signup/` (403 once registration is closed) |

**The ping URLs are the security model.** Each is an unguessable UUID, and anyone holding one can
mark a check up or down. Treat them like passwords.

## The compose file

One service. redu supplies the database.

```yaml
services:
  healthchecks:
    image: healthchecks/healthchecks:v4.3
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      DB: postgres
      DB_HOST: ${PGHOST}
      DB_PORT: ${PGPORT}
      DB_NAME: ${PGDATABASE}
      DB_USER: ${PGUSER}
      DB_PASSWORD: [REDACTED:value]}
      DB_SSLMODE: prefer
      SECRET_KEY: [REDACTED:value]}
      DEBUG: "False"
      SITE_ROOT: ${SITE_ROOT}
      ALLOWED_HOSTS: ${ALLOWED_HOSTS}
      SITE_NAME: ${SITE_NAME}
      REGISTRATION_OPEN: "False"
      SHELL_ENABLED: "False"
      INTEGRATIONS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_IPS: "False"
      DEFAULT_FROM_EMAIL: ${DEFAULT_FROM_EMAIL}
      EMAIL_HOST: ${EMAIL_HOST}
      EMAIL_PORT: ${EMAIL_PORT}
      EMAIL_HOST_USER: ${EMAIL_HOST_USER}
      EMAIL_HOST_PASSWORD: [REDACTED:value]}

`DB: postgres` is the single most important line in that file. Without it the app ignores every
other `DB_*` value, comes up healthy on a SQLite file inside the container, and loses everything
on the next redeploy.

and the five `DB_*` variables have to be mapped by hand.

## Generating the value you must keep

```bash
head -c 64 /dev/urandom | base64 | tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' | head -c 50; echo

## Creating the superuser

Nothing creates an account for you, and registration must be closed before the hostname is
reachable.

EMAIL="$1"
printf 'superuser password (alphanumeric, so nothing needs escaping): ' >&2
read -r PASSWORD

# The engine varies. Find whichever one is running the stack rather than assuming.
ENGINE=docker
sudo docker ps >/dev/null 2>&1 || ENGINE=podman
C=$(sudo $ENGINE ps --format '{{.Names}}' | grep -i health | head -1)

#    satisfied by an error page, and everything after it is therefore meaningful.

  200) echo "FAIL: signup is OPEN. Any stranger can create an account on this instance." >&2; exit 1 ;;

## The three that actually break it

**`DB: postgres`.** Forget it and the app ignores your managed database, quietly uses SQLite, and
names the file after the database you thought you were using.

**`DEBUG` defaults to True in the code.** Not in the sample env file, in `settings.py`. Set it to
False or your error pages hand out your settings.

**`SITE_ROOT` generates every ping URL.** Wrong value, and every URL your user pastes into a
crontab points at `localhost` and silently never reports, which is the one failure this product
exists to prevent.

## Verifying it

Every claim below is gated on the one endpoint that proves both the app and its database.

```bash

HOST="$1"       # healthchecks-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
EMAIL="$2"
printf 'superuser password: ' >&2

#    satisfied by an error page, and everything after it is therefore meaningful.
s=$(mktemp)
code=$(curl -sS -o "$s" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/api/v3/status/")
if [ "$code" = "502" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 502 from the edge, the container is still starting. Re-run in a minute." >&2
  exit 3
fi
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "FAIL: /api/v3/status/ returned $code" >&2; exit 3; }
grep -qx 'OK' "$s" || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 200 but the body is not OK, so this is not Healthchecks." >&2; exit 3; }
echo "OK: the app is up and its database connection works."

Then prove it is really on the managed Postgres, with both halves, because the absence of a SQLite
file means nothing if the command that looked for it never ran:

```bash
set -eu
ENGINE=docker
sudo docker ps >/dev/null 2>&1 || ENGINE=podman
C=$(sudo $ENGINE ps --format '{{.Names}}' | grep -i health | head -1)
[ -n "$C" ] || { echo "no healthchecks container found" >&2; exit 3; }

# Positive half: what the app itself thinks it is connected to.
sudo $ENGINE exec "$C" ./manage.py shell -c \
  "from django.db import connection as c; print('ENGINE', c.vendor, c.settings_dict['NAME'], c.settings_dict['HOST'])" \
  | grep -q '^ENGINE postgresql' || {
    echo "FAIL: the app is NOT on postgresql. Check that DB=postgres is set." >&2; exit 1; }
echo "OK: connected to postgresql on the managed database VM."

# Negative half, meaningful only because the positive half above just passed.
if sudo $ENGINE exec "$C" test -f /opt/healthchecks/hc.sqlite; then
  echo "FAIL: a SQLite file exists in the container. Something wrote to it." >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: no SQLite file, so the fallback never engaged."

## The three that actually break it

**`DB: postgres`.** Forget it and the app ignores your managed database, quietly uses SQLite, and
names the file after the database you thought you were using.

**`DEBUG` defaults to True in the code.** Not in the sample env file, in `settings.py`. Set it to
False or your error pages hand out your settings.

**`SITE_ROOT` generates every ping URL.** Wrong value, and every URL your user pastes into a
crontab points at `localhost` and silently never reports, which is the one failure this product
exists to prevent.
